topic.angle: Why web pages arrive in pieces

card.title: Why web pages arrive in pieces

panels.text: When a server sends you a web page, it does not send one long stream. It cuts the data into small chunks called packets.
Each packet has a header and a payload. The header holds the sender and receiver addresses and the packet's number. The payload is the actual data.
Packets can be routed along different paths, which keeps the network efficient when many people want the same thing. They may arrive out of order.
The twist: that is fine. If one is dropped or corrupted, your computer asks for just that packet again, and the headers put everything back in order.

probes.question: Why is it useful that data travels as small packets?
options: Only missing packets need to be re-requested, and packets can take different paths
Every packet must follow the same single cable
Packets always arrive in the right order

probes.question: True or false: packets can arrive out of order and still be assembled correctly.
